items.title: A 68-year-old client with COPD is increasingly drowsy. Respiratory rate is 8/min, SpO₂ is 86% on prescribed oxygen at 2 L/min, and the client is difficult to arouse. Which action should the nurse take first?

patientInfo.history: Severe COPD; uses long-term oxygen at 2 L/min.

options: Activate rapid response and support airway and ventilation.
Increase oxygen to 15 L/min by nonrebreather and leave the client unattended.
Administer a sedative to reduce respiratory effort.
Encourage oral fluids and reassess in 1 hour.
items.correctAnswer: Activate rapid response and support airway and ventilation.
items.rationale: Bradypnea and declining consciousness indicate impending ventilatory failure, not simply chronic hypoxemia. Immediate emergency assessment and ventilatory support take priority; oxygen delivery should be titrated while avoiding delay in escalation.

items.title: A client at 35 weeks gestation is admitted with severe preeclampsia. Which findings require immediate escalation? Select all that apply.

patientInfo.history: New diagnosis of preeclampsia with severe features.

ehr.assessment: Persistent severe headache, visual spots, and right upper-quadrant pain.

options: Persistent severe headache.
Visual disturbances.
Right upper-quadrant or epigastric pain.
Mild dependent ankle edema at the end of the day.
New clonus or seizure activity.
items.rationale: Neurologic symptoms, visual changes, epigastric or right upper-quadrant pain, and clonus suggest severe disease and risk of eclampsia or HELLP syndrome. Mild dependent edema alone is nonspecific.

items.title: A 4-year-old arrives sitting upright, drooling, febrile, and leaning forward with inspiratory stridor. Which three nursing actions are appropriate?

patientInfo.history: Previously healthy; abrupt onset of fever, sore throat, and difficulty swallowing.

ehr.assessment: Drooling, muffled voice, tripod positioning, inspiratory stridor.

options: Keep the child calm and in the position of comfort.
Notify the airway team and prepare for controlled airway management.
Avoid examining the throat with a tongue depressor.
Lay the child supine for a complete oral examination.
Obtain a throat swab before airway assessment.
correctAnswers: Keep the child calm and in the position of comfort.
Notify the airway team and prepare for controlled airway management.
Avoid examining the throat with a tongue depressor.
items.rationale: The presentation is concerning for epiglottitis with risk of complete airway obstruction. Minimize agitation, avoid pharyngeal manipulation, and obtain expert airway support. Diagnostic procedures must not precipitate obstruction.

items.title: Match each insulin preparation with its usual clinical profile.

patientInfo.history: The nurse is reviewing insulin administration with a client newly prescribed basal-bolus therapy.

columns: Short-acting; may be given IV in selected protocols
Long-acting basal insulin with no pronounced peak

correctAnswers.regular: Short-acting; may be given IV in selected protocols
correctAnswers.glargine: Long-acting basal insulin with no pronounced peak

items.rationale: Lispro is rapid acting and is coordinated with meals. Regular insulin is short acting and is the insulin commonly used IV for DKA protocols. Glargine provides basal coverage and should not be mixed in the same syringe with other insulins.

items.title: For each assessment finding in a client with acute pancreatitis, select all complications it may indicate.

patientInfo.history: Admitted with acute pancreatitis related to gallstones.

ehr.assessment: New crackles, increasing abdominal distention, and reduced urine output.

rows.text: New crackles and increasing oxygen requirement

columns: Renal hypoperfusion or acute kidney injury

renal: Renal hypoperfusion or acute kidney injury

items.rationale: Severe pancreatitis can cause third spacing, systemic inflammation, respiratory complications, and renal hypoperfusion. These findings require prompt escalation and reassessment rather than being considered expected recovery.

patientInfo.history: End-stage kidney disease; missed a scheduled dialysis session.

items.title: Minutes after receiving an IV antibiotic, a client develops generalized urticaria, wheezing, facial swelling, and BP 76/40 mm Hg. Complete the bowtie.

patientInfo.history: Receiving first dose of a prescribed IV antibiotic.

ehr.vitalSigns: BP 76/40 mm Hg; HR 138/min; RR 30/min; SpO₂ 88%.
ehr.assessment: Urticaria, wheezing, facial and tongue swelling.

conditions: Anaphylaxis with airway and circulatory compromise
actions: Stop the triggering infusion and summon emergency assistance
Administer IM epinephrine promptly per emergency protocol and support airway/oxygenation
Continue the antibiotic at a slower rate
monitoring: Airway patency, respiratory effort, and oxygenation
Blood pressure, heart rate, and response to epinephrine

correctAnswers.condition: Anaphylaxis with airway and circulatory compromise
actions: Stop the triggering infusion and summon emergency assistance
Administer IM epinephrine promptly per emergency protocol and support airway/oxygenation
monitoring: Airway patency, respiratory effort, and oxygenation
Blood pressure, heart rate, and response to epinephrine

items.rationale: Rapid-onset skin, airway, and circulatory findings after medication exposure indicate anaphylaxis. IM epinephrine is first-line; stop the trigger, call emergency support, and continuously reassess airway, breathing, and circulation.

items.title: A client reports black stools and coffee-ground emesis. Highlight the findings that indicate hemodynamic compromise: BP 86/50 mm Hg; HR 128/min; cool clammy skin; capillary refill 4 seconds; hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL; chronic heartburn for 5 years.

patientInfo.history: History of peptic ulcer disease and intermittent NSAID use.

ehr.assessment: Melena, coffee-ground emesis, cool clammy skin, capillary refill 4 seconds.

items.rationale: Hypotension, tachycardia, cool clammy skin, delayed capillary refill, and low hemoglobin in the setting of gastrointestinal bleeding suggest significant blood loss and impaired perfusion. Chronic heartburn is relevant history but does not establish current hemodynamic compromise.

items.title: A child weighs 18 kg. The prescription is 10 mg/kg of a medication. The oral solution contains 120 mg per 5 mL. How many mL should be administered for one dose? Round to the nearest tenth.

patientInfo.history: Weight verified at 18 kg; medication prescribed as a single oral dose.

ehr.medication: Prescribed dose 10 mg/kg; concentration 120 mg/5 mL.

items.rationale: Required dose: 18 kg × 10 mg/kg = 180 mg. Concentration: 120 mg ÷ 5 mL = 24 mg/mL. Volume: 180 mg ÷ 24 mg/mL = 7.5 mL. Verify the medication, weight, dose range, and measuring device before administration.

items.title: A client being evaluated for chest pain has the following trend: 0900 pain 3/10, HR 88/min, BP 132/78 mm Hg; 0915 pain 7/10, HR 108/min, BP 148/86 mm Hg; 0930 pain 8/10 with diaphoresis and new ST-segment elevation. What is the priority interpretation and response?

patientInfo.history: Hypertension and tobacco use; chest discomfort began 45 minutes ago.

ehr.trend: 0900: pain 3/10, HR 88, BP 132/78. 0915: pain 7/10, HR 108, BP 148/86. 0930: pain 8/10, diaphoresis, new ST elevation.

items.correctAnswer: The client may be experiencing an acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction; activate the STEMI/emergency pathway immediately and prepare for urgent reperfusion evaluation.
items.rationale: Worsening ischemic chest pain with diaphoresis and new ST elevation is a time-critical STEMI pattern. Activate the emergency pathway, obtain/continue ECG monitoring, establish access, and prepare for urgent reperfusion; do not delay escalation for routine reassessment.
